# Introduction and reader's guide {#sec-introduction}

Affine Toda field theories are a family of two-dimensional quantum field theories, one for each affine Kac–Moody algebra $\hat g$. They are integrable, so many of their properties can be computed exactly, and they are rich enough to display most of the phenomena of interacting quantum field theory: particles and bound states, solitons and breathers, strong–weak duality, quantum-group symmetry, integrable boundaries and, at imaginary coupling, non-unitarity. This book introduces them to a reader who knows quantum field theory but has not met affine Toda theory, Kac–Moody algebras or quantum groups, and leads that reader to current research.

## About this book {#sec-about}

**Editorial model and AI drafting.** Gustav Delius is the coordinating editor. Most of the text and the supporting code were drafted by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, working from outlines, source papers and briefs assembled by the coordinating editor. Further Claude, Codex and Gemini instances have been used for automated critique and consistency checks, not as human referees. The prose, many of the proofs and the numerical checks are machine-drafted, and errors may remain. Where a result matters to you, check the proof, and where the book gives a script (`textbook_code/`, `foundations_code/`, `soliton_rmatrix_code/`; see the [guide to the supporting code](appendices/C-code.qmd)), run it.

**Subject-matter validation.** Niall MacKay and Gerard Watts are the first subject-matter validators. This is only the beginning of the list: the project aims to invite cited researchers working on affine Toda theory to validate the book's representation of their own research. Each validator checks only that limited scope. Listing a validator does not imply that they have reviewed or endorsed the rest of the book, and this subject-matter validation is not a substitute for independent peer review.

**Prerequisites.** Quantum field theory at the level of a first graduate course (path integrals, perturbation theory, renormalization, the S-matrix), finite-dimensional Lie algebras at the level of $su(n)$, and complex analysis. Everything else is developed in the text.

**Status.** All chapters are drafted. Parts I–IV, Parts VII–VIII and the textbook chapters of Parts V–VI have not yet been refereed by a human specialist. The record of what has been checked, and how, is in the repository (`briefs/referee_textbook.md`, for Part VII `briefs/referee_half_line_*.md`, for Part VIII `briefs/part8_defects_status.md` and `briefs/referee_defects_*.md`, and `textbook_code/`).

## Presentation and new results {#sec-new-results}

Parts I–IV, Parts VII and VIII, and the introductory chapters of Parts V and VI present established material. We have rewritten it in a common notation and with consistent conventions, and have added exercises, figures and some derivations that the original papers omit, but the results are those of the literature cited in each chapter's *Notes and references*. Parts V, VI and IX contain original results. Elsewhere, re-deriving the material in one set of conventions, with a check script for every key formula, produced new results and corrections: one in chapter 11, and several on the half-line (Part VII) and on defects (Part VIII). We list them all below, so that a reader can tell what is new. From Part V on, the main statements carry a status label:

- **[Theorem]**, with a complete proof given here;
- **[Proposition, sketch]**, with a proof outline that a specialist could complete;
- **[Established]**, proved or computed in the cited literature (**[Established; reformulated]** when we restate it in a different form);
- **[Numerical]**, checked numerically by a script in the repository but not proved;
- **[Conjecture]**, with the supporting evidence stated.

**Original results.** Each item gives the status of the result and ends with the statement that contains it, or with the section when no single statement does.

::: {.original-results}
**Classical solitons (chapter 11).**

- **[Theorem, given additivity of the higher charges]** A selection rule from the antilinear symmetry $\Theta$. If the asymptotic data of a classical solution are $\Theta$-invariant, every conserved charge is real or imaginary according to its parity under $\Theta$, and the energy and momentum are real. The reality results of Olive, Turok and Underwood, of Zhu and Caldi and of Freeman, and the complex energies of Khastgir and Sasaki, fit this one criterion, and the earlier restriction to "good" solutions becomes a symmetry statement. Singular solutions are not covered (@sec-reality-energy-momentum).

**Semiclassical quantization of complex solitons (chapters 17–19).**

- **[Proposition, sketch]** Picard–Lefschetz theory applied to the saddles of affine Toda theory. Static soliton saddles alone cannot fill the quantum-group multiplets of topological charges (@prp-static-saddles).
- **[Conjecture]** The static solitons and the complexified two-soliton bound states have nonzero intersection numbers exactly in the sectors needed to fill the multiplets (@cnj-missing-charge).
- **[Part theorem given (D), part conjecture]** The counting rule. Eigenvalues of the non-Hermitian fluctuation operator are counted with algebraic multiplicity, which is the net order (zeros minus poles) of the product of the transmission factors. This resolves the disagreement between the one-loop $c_n^{(1)}$ masses of MacKay and Watts and of Delius and Grisaru, and that between the one-loop and the exact $b_n^{(1)}$ masses (@cnj-counting-rule).
- **[Theorem]** Wherever the fluctuation solutions are reflectionless and species-diagonal near an eigenvalue, the zeros of the transmission factors give Jordan chains whose lengths are the orders of the zeros (@thm-jordan-chains).
- **[Theorem]** A transmission-factor formula for one-loop masses. It extends the formula of Cahill, Comtet and Glauber to several channels, to poles as well as zeros, and to complex solitons. The proof reduces each mass level to reflectionless Pöschl–Teller wells, whose heat traces in a single real channel are known (@prp-one-loop-mass).
- **[Theorem given (D)]** The fluctuation solutions about the solitons of $d_n^{(1)}$, $e_n^{(1)}$ and their foldings have the Hirota form, given a degree bound (D). The bound is checked numerically for $d_4^{(1)},\dots,d_8^{(1)}$, $e_{6,7,8}^{(1)}$ and 19 foldings (@prp-hirota-form).
- **[Numerical]** One-loop masses of the folded solitons, for the families and ranks tabulated in chapter 19. With the counting rule, all soliton mass ratios of a family follow one floating Coxeter number (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded).
- **[Numerical, one loop]** A prediction of the four $f_4^{(1)}$ soliton masses (@sec-one-loop-masses-folded).

**Soliton S-matrices (chapters 23–27).** Among the non-simply-laced theories, $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$, $e_6^{(2)}$ and $f_4^{(1)}$ had no soliton S-matrix in the literature.

- **[Numerical for $n=3,4$; Conjecture for $n\ge5$]** The S-matrix of the spinor solitons of $c_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge3$, built on the R-matrix of Delius, Gould and Zhang, and the complete $c_3^{(1)}$ S-matrix. The soliton masses agree with one loop (@sec-sm-cn).
- **[Numerical for $n=3,4$; Conjecture for $n\ge5$]** The S-matrix of the spinor solitons of $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$, $n\ge3$. The soliton masses agree with one loop and with the lattice model of Vernier, Jacobsen and Saleur (@sec-sm-a2n).
- **[Numerical]** The S-matrix of the $\mathbf{26}$ solitons of $e_6^{(2)}$ (@sec-sm-e6).
- **[Numerical]** The $f_4^{(1)}$ obstruction. A candidate amplitude for the $\mathbf{27}$ solitons satisfies the axioms, but the one-loop soliton masses exclude it, and no finite CDD factor repairs it. The soliton S-matrix of $f_4^{(1)}$ remains open (@sec-sm-f4).
- **[Theorem, given a unitary and real-analytic scalar factor]** For the RSOS-restricted $a_2^{(1)}$ theory, the perturbed $W_3(p,p')$ model with $p\ge4$, the S-matrix of the fundamental kinks is Hermitian analytic and unitary exactly when $p'\equiv\pm1\pmod p$. With the breathers included, only $p'=p+1$ gives a unitary S-matrix (@prp-rsos-kinks).
- **[Conjecture]** A general criterion: an RSOS-restricted affine Toda theory has a unitary S-matrix exactly when its restricted S-matrix, breathers included, is Hermitian analytic in some basis (@cnj-unitary-rsos).

**Half-line (chapters 28–35).**

- **[Conjecture]** The Neumann boundary of $a_n^{(1)}$ has the non-diagonal soliton reflection matrix with $s=+1$, and the diagonal one belongs to the uniform boundary $C_j\equiv+1$, as Delius and Gandenberger had assigned it. This contradicts the reading of Delius and MacKay's first-order computation. For $n=2$ the Neumann half is Gandenberger's (@cnj-neumann-coideal).
- **[Numerical]** The soliton derivation of the Neumann particle amplitudes, given @cnj-neumann-coideal and the continuation in the coupling, for $n\le4$; in the literature it was done only for $a_2^{(1)}$ (@prp-an-nondiagonal-scalar).
- **[Numerical]** For $n\le7$ the amplitudes of the $s=-1$ matrix are dual to the $C\equiv-1$ proposal of Corrigan, Dorey, Rietdijk and Sasaki. This extends an observation of Gandenberger (@sec-neumann-duality).
- **[Numerical for $n\le7$; Proposition, sketch in general]** The allowed quantum boundary parameters of $a_n^{(1)}$. A reflection matrix for the vector solitons exists only when all $\hat\epsilon_j=0$ or all $\hat\epsilon_j^2=1/\big((1-q)(1-q^{-1})\big)$. This corrects the constraint of Delius and MacKay; the value was first published by Baseilhac and Belliard (@prp-an-k-existence).
- **[Theorem]** The quantum Serre relation of the boundary coideal for arbitrary parameters, with its Cartan term computed exactly. The term vanishes exactly at the value above, which Baseilhac and Belliard found as the condition for their generalized $q$-Onsager relations (@prp-serre-obstruction).
- **[Proposition, sketch]** The coideals with these parameters are not quantum symmetric pairs in Kolb's sense, but images of the standard one under a character twist, as Dobson and Kolb found for Kolb's nonstandard parameters (@prp-one-dim-modules).
- **[Theorem]** Dirichlet conditions on all components are not classically integrable for any $g^{(1)}\ne a_1^{(1)}$, as Corrigan had remarked without proof (@prp-no-dirichlet).
- **[Numerical]** The classically integrable boundary conditions of @tbl-durham include a new branch for $c_2^{(1)}=b_2^{(1)}$, and correct those of Bowcock, Corrigan, Dorey and Rietdijk for $g_2^{(1)}$ and $d_4^{(3)}$ (@prp-durham).

**Defects (chapters 36–43).**

- **[Theorem for $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_3^{(1)}$; Proposition, sketch for all $a_r^{(1)}$]** Both the spin $+2$ and the spin $-2$ charges survive both types of defect of $a_r^{(1)}$, contrary to Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon and to Penati and Polvara. The obstruction they found vanishes for every $r$ (@prp-spin-two).
- **[Theorem; Numerical for the second Borel subalgebra of type I$_+$]** A sine-Gordon jump defect, seen as a boundary of the doubled theory, is not invariant under any twisted diagonal coideal built from a Hopf twist, so @cnj-twisted-diagonal is refuted. It keeps a diagonal Borel subalgebra and a second one twisted by charge conjugation (@prp-diagonal-borel).
- **[Theorem]** For every $a_r^{(1)}$, $r\ge2$, and generic $q$, the type-I$_-$ jump defect keeps a diagonal Borel subalgebra and a second one twisted by the rotation of the Dynkin diagram, and no other twist of this kind (@prp-dpt-doubled).
- **[Numerical]** The lowest breather of every species of $a_2^{(1)}$, $a_3^{(1)}$ and $a_4^{(1)}$ crosses a type-I$_-$ defect with its classical transmission factor at every coupling. Corrigan and Zambon found this for $a_2^{(1)}$ (@prp-lightest-breather-universal).
- **[Numerical]** In the book's conventions, crossing of the $a_r^{(1)}$ transmission matrices, $r=2,3,4$, selects the sign of $q$ when $h$ is odd, and only together with the conjugation matrix when $h$ is even (@prp-transmission-crossing).
- **[Conjecture]** The particles of the real-coupling $a_r^{(1)}$ theory cross a type-I defect without reflection, with transmission factors obtained from the soliton transmission matrices by continuation in the coupling (@cnj-transmission-continuation).

**Foundations of the non-unitary theory (chapters 44–49).**

- **[Theorem]** A lattice regularization of every imaginary-coupling theory whose partition function is a convergent sum of positive Coulomb-gas weights, so that the complex action gives no sign problem (@thm-bounded-weight; @thm-coulomb-gas).
- **[Theorem]** The lattice transfer matrix is self-adjoint for an indefinite (Krein) inner product and commutes with the antilinear symmetry $\Theta$ (@thm-krein-transfer).
- **[Theorem]** The finite-volume vacuum energy of the lattice theory is real (@thm-vacuum-energy).
- **[Theorem]** A finite-volume continuum limit for every algebra below the first collapse threshold $\beta^2_{\rm UV}$, with Wick ordering site by site, and a divergence at and above it. These proofs have not yet been checked independently (@prp-continuum-limit; @prp-uv-divergence).
- **[Proposition, sketch]** A Krein-unitarity criterion. On a Krein space, and given asymptotic completeness, the eigenvalues of the S-matrices and of the Bethe–Yang transfer matrices are pure phases or come in pairs $(s,1/\bar s)$ (@prp-krein-unitarity).
- **[Theorem]** Given a unitary and real-analytic scalar factor, the S-matrix of the fundamental solitons of $a_n^{(1)}$ is Krein-unitary, without any assumption of asymptotic completeness, and so is an integrable light-cone regularization (@prp-krein-fundamental; @prp-krein-regularization).
- **[Numerical]** A sector-by-sector classification of where $\Theta$ is unbroken. It corrects the two-kink statement of Takács and Watts for $a_2^{(2)}$ (@sec-sector-status).
- **[Theorem]** Graded exchange statistics of the solitons is a twist of the Bethe–Yang equations by a Bloch angle (@prp-exchange-twist).
- **[Theorem]** A no-go lemma: a non-real energy, a Jordan block, or a transfer-matrix eigenvalue off the unit circle rules out every positive inner product that would make the theory unitary. It yields the list of consequences of unitarity that no change of description can restore in the unrestricted theories of rank $r\ge2$, @sec-properties-cannot-be-rescued, each with its own status (@lem-no-go).
:::

The checks also found errors and misprints in published papers, among them several formulas of Corrigan and Zambon's $a_r^{(1)}$ defect papers. Each is corrected in the chapter's notes, and @sec-app-corrections collects them all.

**Presentation of known material.** The book also gathers, in one notation, results that the literature scatters: factorized scattering and sine-Gordon (Part I), root systems, affine algebras, quantum groups and R-matrices (Part II), classical solitons and Hirota solutions (Part III), the exact particle S-matrices, the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz and form factors at real coupling (Part IV), the quantum-group symmetry and bootstrap construction of soliton S-matrices (chapters 20–22), and the theory on the half-line: integrable boundary conditions, solitons reflected by the boundary, the boundary quantum-group symmetry and the reflection matrices it determines, and their place in the theory of quantum symmetric pairs (Part VII), and the theory with integrable defects: their scattering axioms, the defect conditions as frozen Bäcklund transformations, and the Borel quantum-group symmetry and transmission matrices of the defects (Part VIII).

Statements labelled **[Theorem]** have complete proofs in the text but, being new, have not been checked by anyone outside the project. The Part IX continuum-limit theorems in particular await independent checking.

## Why affine Toda theory matters {#sec-why-atft-matters}

For each affine Kac–Moody algebra $\hat g$ there is a Lagrangian field theory of $r=\operatorname{rank}g$ scalars with exponential interactions, the affine Toda field theory. Its Lagrangian is $\mathcal L=\tfrac12\partial_\mu\vec\phi\cdot\partial^\mu\vec\phi-V(\vec\phi)$, with $\vec\phi\in\mathbb R^r$ and one of the two potentials

$$
V_{\rm real}=\frac{m^2}{\beta^2}\sum_jn_j\left(e^{\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}-1\right),\qquad
V_{\rm imag}=-\frac{m^2}{\beta^2}\sum_jn_j\left(e^{i\beta\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}-1\right).
$$

The sums run over the $r+1$ simple roots $\vec\alpha_0,\dots,\vec\alpha_r\in\mathbb R^r$ of $\hat g$, the $n_j$ are positive integers called Kac labels, $m$ sets the mass scale and $\beta>0$ is the coupling. Part II defines the roots and labels (@sec-affine-dynkin), and Part III takes up the theory again from these potentials (-@eq-imaginary-potential). Until then two facts suffice. The labels satisfy $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$, so $\vec\phi=0$ is a stationary point of both potentials. For the smallest algebra, $a_1^{(1)}$, one has $r=1$, $\alpha_1=-\alpha_0=\sqrt2$ and $n_0=n_1=1$, and the two potentials are those of sinh-Gordon and sine-Gordon theory (@sec-sg-dictionary).

These theories have been a laboratory for several central ideas in two-dimensional quantum field theory:

- exact factorized S-matrices and the bootstrap [@zz1979; @braden1990];
- the geometry of root systems in scattering (Dorey's fusing rule [@dorey1991]);
- strong–weak coupling duality [@braden1990; @dgz1992];
- solitons with quantum-group symmetry [@bernard1991; @hollowood1993b];
- integrable boundary conditions and reflection matrices [@gz1994; @bcdr1995; @delius_mackay2003];
- integrable perturbations of conformal field theories [@zamolodchikov1989; @eguchi1989; @hollowood1989];
- the ODE/IM correspondence [@lukyanov2010; @dorey2013].

The theories come in two regimes.

- **Real coupling.** The theory is an ordinary unitary QFT with a unique vacuum and $r$ massive particles.
- **Imaginary coupling.** The potential is periodic and complex. There are infinitely many degenerate vacua, solitons interpolating between them, and breathers. These are the theories that describe perturbed (W-algebra) minimal models after quantum-group restriction, and they carry the richest physics.

@fig-two-regimes shows the two kinds of potential for $a_1^{(1)}$ and $a_2^{(1)}$.

![The two regimes. (a) For $a_1^{(1)}$, in the sine-Gordon normalization of @sec-sg-dictionary, the real-coupling potential has a single minimum and the imaginary-coupling potential has infinitely many. A kink runs between neighbouring minima. (b) For $a_2^{(1)}$ the vacua of the imaginary-coupling theory form a hexagonal lattice, shown on the real part of $V_{\rm imag}$ (its imaginary part also vanishes at the vacua).](figures/intro_f2_potentials.svg){#fig-two-regimes fig-alt="Left: the cosh potential with one minimum and the cosine potential with infinitely many minima, with an arrow for a kink between adjacent minima. Right: a contour plot of the real part of the imaginary-coupling potential of a_2^(1) over the plane of the two fields, with its minima at the points of a triangular lattice."}

The theories are not only of historical interest. They are rich enough to show generic phenomena of quantum field theory, yet solvable enough that claims about them can be checked exactly. Five features keep them current.

- **A family, not a single model.** There is one theory for each affine algebra, and results come with Lie-theoretic structure: Dorey's fusing rule, Perron–Frobenius masses, Lie duality. A general claim about integrable or massive two-dimensional QFT can therefore be tested across a whole family, not in one example.
- **Exact benchmarks.** At real coupling the S-matrices are known for every algebra, together with the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz, form factors and the exact mass–coupling relation (@sec-real-coupling). New methods are calibrated against them. Recent examples are tree-level integrability for every ATFT, derived from properties of root systems [@dorey_polvara2022], one-loop integrability of the simply-laced theories [@polvara2023], and the comparison of one-loop amplitudes with the bootstrap S-matrices for the whole simply-laced class [@fabri_polvara2024].
- **A non-unitary QFT with structure.** The imaginary-coupling theories are the field-theoretic parents of non-unitary perturbed minimal and W-algebra models. We argue that their non-unitarity is organised by a Krein structure and an antilinear $PT$-type symmetry $\Theta$, and is not a pathology. That is the question non-Hermitian physics now asks of many systems (@sec-connections-current-research).
- **Unfinished business.** The soliton S-matrix of $f_4^{(1)}$ is still missing, and those of $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $e_6^{(2)}$ are constructed in Part VI, though not for every soliton species (@sec-imaginary-coupling-quantum-theory). The disagreements over one-loop soliton masses needed a new counting rule to resolve (@sec-semiclassics). The missing-topological-charge problem is open, and static complex saddles cannot resolve it (@sec-which-saddles-contribute). On the half-line, particle reflection amplitudes are known only for $a_n^{(1)}$, and those of the Neumann boundary have been derived from the solitons only for $a_2^{(1)}$ (@sec-boundary-open-problems). Open problems in a theory whose surroundings are this well mapped are unusually well posed.
- **A meeting point of mathematics and physics.** Quantum affine algebras and their R-matrices, quantum symmetric pairs and their K-matrices, Hirota tau-functions, Coulomb gases and Picard–Lefschetz theory all act on the same model. Progress in any one of them tends to have consequences here.

## How this book is organised {#sec-reader-guide}

The book has nine parts.

- **Part I** collects the physical background: factorized scattering in two dimensions, sine-Gordon theory as the rank-one template, and the non-Hermitian quantum mechanics needed for the imaginary-coupling theories.
- **Part II** collects the algebraic background: root systems, affine Kac–Moody algebras, quantum groups and R-matrices.
- **Part III** treats the classical field theory: Lagrangians, integrability, solitons and the reality of their energies.
- **Part IV** treats the quantum theory at real coupling, where the exact particle S-matrices are known for every algebra.
- **Part V** treats the semiclassical quantization of the complex solitons of the imaginary-coupling theories.
- **Part VI** treats their exact soliton S-matrices, including the constructions for $c_n^{(1)}$, $a_{2n-1}^{(2)}$ and $e_6^{(2)}$ and the open case $f_4^{(1)}$.
- **Part VII** restricts the theories to a half-line: integrable boundary conditions, solitons and their mirror images, the remnant of quantum-group symmetry that a boundary leaves unbroken and its place in the theory of quantum symmetric pairs, and the exact reflection amplitudes of solitons and particles.
- **Part VIII** puts a defect into the theory, a line that particles and solitons cross without being reflected: the scattering axioms of transmitting defects, sine-Gordon and $a_r^{(1)}$ defects as Bäcklund transformations frozen at a point, the solitons that cross them, their Borel quantum-group symmetry and transmission matrices, and the relation between defects and boundaries.
- **Part IX** asks whether the imaginary-coupling theories exist as quantum field theories, and answers: yes, as non-unitary ones.

Parts I–IV are textbook material. Parts V, VI and IX present research results, many of them new. Part VII presents the theory on the half-line, developed in the research literature since 1993, in textbook form, and Part VIII does the same for integrable defects, studied since 1994.

- *A course on integrable field theory:* chapters 2–3, 5–6, 9–10, 12–14, then 20–22. This covers sine-Gordon, the classical theory, the particle S-matrices and the known soliton S-matrices.
- *A course on quantum groups in field theory:* chapters 2–3 and 5–8, then 20–22 and 27.
- *Integrable boundaries:* chapters 2–3, 7–10 and 13, then Part VII, consulting chapters 20–21 for the quantum-group method.
- *Integrable defects:* chapters 2–3, 7–11 and 20–21, then 28–32, then Part VIII, consulting chapters 13 and 33–35 for its last chapters.
- *Non-unitary quantum field theory:* chapters 2–4, 9–11, then Part IX, consulting Parts V–VI as needed.

**What Part I borrows from Part II.** Part I uses some algebraic terms before Part II defines them. They appear in statements about general affine Toda theories, which a first reading can take on trust, and the sine-Gordon case of @sec-sine-gordon needs none of them in more than its simplest form. In brief:

- **Affine Kac–Moody algebra** $\hat g=X_n^{(k)}$: an infinite-dimensional extension of a simple Lie algebra, untwisted for $k=1$ and twisted for $k=2,3$. All the theory needs from it is its simple roots $\vec\alpha_j$, its Kac labels $n_j$ and its **affine Dynkin diagram**, a graph with one node per simple root (@sec-affine-algebras).
- **Cartan matrix, Coxeter number $h$, exponents**: the Cartan matrix is the matrix $a_{ij}=2\vec\alpha_i\cdot\vec\alpha_j/\vec\alpha_i^2$ of the simple roots; the Coxeter number is $h=\sum_jn_j$; and the exponents are a set of positive integers attached to each algebra (for untwisted $\hat g=g^{(1)}$, $r$ integers between 1 and $h-1$), which become the spins of the conserved charges (@sec-roots, @sec-weyl-coxeter, @sec-conserved-charges).
- **Perron–Frobenius eigenvector**: the eigenvector of the Cartan matrix of $g$ with positive components; in the simply-laced theories the particle masses are proportional to its components (@sec-perron-frobenius).
- **Dorey's fusing rule**: a criterion, in terms of the Coxeter element of the Weyl group, for which three-point couplings of particles are nonzero (@sec-dorey-rule).
- **Duality of algebras and Lie duality**: reversing the arrows of an affine Dynkin diagram gives the dual algebra $\hat g^\vee$; "Lie duality" relates the soliton masses of $g^{(1)}$ to the particle masses of $(g^\vee)^{(1)}$ (@sec-affine-folding).
- **Quantum affine algebras** $U_q(\hat g)$: deformations of the symmetry algebra of $\hat g$. They are Hopf algebras, whose coproduct says how a symmetry acts on multi-particle states and whose antipode gives crossing. Their **evaluation representations** are finite-dimensional representations depending on a spectral parameter, which becomes the rapidity (@sec-quantum-groups).
- **IRF (RSOS) basis and quantum-group restriction**: a change of basis from soliton labels to sequences of vacua, after which, when $q$ is a root of unity, all but finitely many vacua can be discarded consistently (@sec-irf, @sec-qg-restriction). The restricted theories are perturbed minimal models of Virasoro or of $W$-algebras, the conformal field theories with higher-spin symmetry currents (@sec-perturbed-minimal).

## Conventions {#sec-conventions}

We use units with $\hbar=c=1$ and the metric signature $(+,-)$. Rapidities are written $\theta$, and two-particle amplitudes depend on the rapidity difference (@sec-rapidities).

Roots are normalized so that the longest roots of the finite algebra have squared length 2, as in @sec-lie-algebraic-data. Some of the literature instead gives the longest root of a twisted algebra $X_n^{(k)}$ squared length $2k$; its coupling is then $\beta_{\rm lit}^2=\beta^2/k$, and we convert whenever we quote such results. The coupling $\beta$ is always real and positive. "Real coupling" and "imaginary coupling" refer to the two potentials $V_{\rm real}$ and $V_{\rm imag}$ of @sec-why-atft-matters, restated as (-@eq-imaginary-potential), not to the sign of $\beta^2$. For $a_1^{(1)}$ our $\beta$ is related to the conventional sine-Gordon coupling by $\beta_{\rm SG}^2=2\beta^2$ (@sec-sine-gordon).

In Part VII the field lives on the half-line $x\le0$, with the boundary at $x=0$. A boundary potential, with one coefficient $C_j$ for each simple root, fixes the boundary condition (@sec-boundary-potential). In Part VIII the defect sits at $x=0$, with the field $\vec\phi$ on $x<0$ and $\vec\psi$ on $x>0$ and the defect parameter $\sigma=e^{-\theta_d}$, $\theta_d$ the defect rapidity; the transmission matrix maps $V\otimes\mathcal W\to\mathcal W\otimes V$, $\mathcal W$ the space of defect states, with the tensor factors in spatial order (@sec-defect-lagrangian, @sec-defect-scattering).
